items.question: Why do you think a computer for dataflow problems needs to be reconfigurable?
items.object: Reconfigurable dataflow computers
items.answer: We have a data flow problem, right? So let's build a data flow computer, right? So let's build a computer that matches the data flows as represented by the algorithm in the hardware. So why does it need to be reconfigurable? Well, because you don't have one graph, right? You reconfigure it.

The response explains that a dataflow computer needs reconfigurability because it must accommodate different dataflow graphs.

items.question: What do you prioritize when designing computing architectures for AI inference?
items.object: Computing architectures for AI inference
items.answer: Our focus is on how you do very efficient, fast inference on big models as energy efficiently as possible. The focus has been on very large models, models with trillions of parameters that can fit in a single rack, on models that are good for agentic solutions where you've got hundreds of agents that potentially all need to work together and switch between these agents with very low latency, and then very fast inference because you have interactive environments that you want to support multiple LM model calls sequentially for chain of thought kinds of reasoning, or because you've got a workflow that requires lots of calls.

items.question: How do you think machine learning’s computational structure should shape the design of its hardware?
items.object: Data flow computer architecture for machine learning
items.answer: Well, it comes basically from thinking about how you take the computational paradigm that comes from machine learning and implement it in hardware. You think about designing an AI or ML algorithm, and you do it in your favorite domain specific language framework. These days everybody's favorite is PyTorch. Once you write your algorithm in PyTorch, what you get is what computer scientists would call a data flow graph. The data flow graph is a graph which has nodes and edges, because all graphs have nodes and edges. The nodes in this case are kernels of computation like matrix multiply or convolution or softmax, or maybe your favorite kernel that you came up with to support your specialized model. The edges are basically tensor data, matrices, the flow between these nodes. There's a famous computer architect named Jim Smith, and he designed Cray computers back in the day. His favorite quote that I often use is, if you have a vector problem, and most of the problems were vector problems, then you should build a vector computer. So, we have a data flow problem, so let's build a data flow computer. Let's build a computer that matches the data flows as represented by the algorithm in the hardware.

items.question: How do you distinguish reconfigurable dataflow from traditional computer architectures?
items.object: Reconfigurable dataflow versus traditional computer architectures
items.answer: Do you fetch an instruction every cycle and decide what to do, or do you configure your hardware and leave it that way for the whole program? That's the difference, right? That's one difference. The other difference I think is a kind of technical issue but also is very important, which is how do you synchronize the computation? You've got parallel computation, and the way that parallel computation typically works is the way that you communicate is through a single address space called shared memory. Whenever you do this, you need some sort of synchronization to make sure that you know that the data that one thread put in the memory is ready for the next thread to go pick up. So locks, barriers, all this other stuff. Reconfigurable data flow has none of that. You don't have any of that. So this is a huge benefit.

items.question: Why do you see data flow tags as a good fit for communication between computational kernels on a chip?
items.object: Synchronization and communication using data flow tags
items.answer: The way that you do the synchronization is by using data flow tags. You've got hardware mechanisms that essentially are tokens, which determine when data is ready. I send you a stream of data and I've got some tokens there which you can look at and decide when the data is ready. That's the way that you do communication, and it matches very nicely with this model of the graph where one kernel does a computation and it generates data and it sends that to another kernel which is executing on a different piece of the chip.

items.question: Why do you see reconfigurable dataflow architectures as particularly well suited to large language model inference?
items.object: Reconfigurable dataflow architectures for large language model inference
items.answer: It turns out the architecture was very well suited for LLMs, fundamentally especially for inference. Inference was something that we saw was really going to be a bottleneck. If you think about inference, it's fundamentally constrained by the memory bandwidth. I should back up and say when I talked to you in 2018, this idea was pretty theoretical. Now we have five generations of chip. The chip that we currently have in the market is called the SN40L, which is a 100 billion transistor, 5 nanometer chip. It has three tiers of memory: half a gigabyte of memory on chip, 64 GB of HBM connected to the accelerator, and high capacity memory, 1.5 terabytes of DDR. This is unique in that most accelerators do not have that high capacity memory. If you think about doing inference on a large language model, it's fundamentally constrained by the memory bandwidth to fetch the parameters and to fetch the KV cache from the HBM. That's the limit. What you want to do then is make sure that you don't send any extraneous data that should not be necessary over that highly constrained, critical resource, that HBM bandwidth. Reconfigurable data flow does this by—you think, go back to your streaming idea. If you take an LLM model, let's take a simple one like Llama 3.1 8B, an 8 billion parameter model. It's got these decoders, and it's got 32 decoders, which are essentially the same operation. What you can do is take that whole decoder and map it onto a set of 16 RDU chips in space.

items.question: How do you use reconfigurable data flow units to keep an LLM decoder’s internal data from crossing the HBM accelerator boundary?
items.object: Mapping an LLM decoder across reconfigurable data flow units
items.answer: We call it a reconfigurable data flow architecture, and the chip we call a reconfigurable data flow unit, RDU. So take 16 of these RDUs and take the one decoder and map it in space across all those chips. Now it's resident on your system, and then to generate the tokens, you just loop through that 16 times, and no data ever goes between the different components of the decoder, ever crosses the HBM accelerator boundary.

items.question: Why do you favor asynchronous dataflow execution for keeping AI inference hardware busy?
items.object: Asynchronous dataflow execution for AI inference
items.answer: The other thing that we do comes back to this idea of synchronization and making sure that the synchronization is very low overhead. As you know, in any computer system, you have to make sure that the critical resource is used 100% of the time because that's going to limit your performance. The performance limiter for inference is, as we've just discussed, HBM bandwidth for the parameters and the KV cache. What you want to do is make sure that you never have that interface idle, and you overlap the computation happening in the RDUs with the memory access on the HBM and the communication across chip to the other RDUs. You keep all of this—it's like everything everywhere all at once. You want everything to be busy all at the same time, and you want to make sure that you use that interface to the HBM all the time. What we do is we can achieve a fraction of busy time on the RDU two to three times higher than GPUs can achieve because we have this data flow idea of asynchronous execution of all the components. There's no sequential instruction access. One of the other things alluding to your earlier question of why this is different: the problem with sequential instruction execution—it has a benefit, which is humans can understand what's going on. The downside is it keeps things sequential. What you want is asynchrony. GPUs are starting to get into this, but we've taken it to the extreme in data flow. It's everything all at once, all the time. It's all happening at the same time, much like you would in a hardware system, and there's nothing keeping us from keeping things busy.

items.question: Why do you see explicit prefetching as unnecessary for keeping high-bandwidth memory busy in a dataflow design?
items.object: Prefetching and HBM utilization in dataflow computing
items.answer: I'd say it comes naturally once you design things in this data flow manner. You don't have to prefetch, because you naturally have prefetching going on. That unit accessing the HBM is working independently at the rate at which the HBM can go. You don't have to prefetch.

items.question: How do you approach mapping an AI model to a dataflow architecture to make the best use of HBM bandwidth?
items.object: Mapping AI models to a dataflow architecture to use HBM bandwidth efficiently
items.answer: Part of the trick is how we're going to map the model to our architecture. We're going to map it in such a way that we make sure that the HBM bandwidth is the limiter for the data we need to move. The idea is we don't move any data that we shouldn't have to using the HBM bandwidth. We only use the HBM bandwidth for the absolutely necessary data. A GPU puts intermediate data between the kernels that flows back and forth the GPU. That's wasted bandwidth. We don't do any of that because we've got these data flow mechanisms that move the data between the kernels on chip and between chips using chip to chip interconnect. Then we also make sure that that critical resource is used at the highest utilization that we can muster, which is upwards of 90%, which GPUs cannot touch for multiple reasons.

items.question: How do you think about mapping an AI model to your dataflow architecture to get the best inference performance?
items.object: Mapping AI models to a dataflow architecture
items.answer: We start with PyTorch models, and PyTorch gives us a graph of operators. We have an implementation of these operators in our environment. If you think about these operators, you can describe them as either GEMMs or some custom operation. This custom operation could be described using a MapReduce paradigm. We've got a Python environment that allows you to describe specialized operators using MapReduce. Now you've got a set of kernels, and the question is how should you fuse these kernels together to create a representation that can be mapped? You need to parallelize within the chip by splitting up the tensors. You might want to reduce the size of things by tiling, just by taking the tile computation, thinking back to what you had to do manually in something like FlashAttention. You also want to think about how you shard the computation across multiple chips. Our compiler has mechanisms for you to specify what you want based on the tensors. This is all about the tensors. You take a tensor and say, am I going to tile the tensor? Am I going to parallelize a tensor? Am I going to shard the tensor? That's the way you get the mapping. Now you have something that can map to your machine, which is a collection of RDUs. The whole goal is there'll be some performance tweaking, but at the end of the day what you're trying to do is make sure that you are using the critical resource, if it's inference, HBM bandwidth, to the maximum extent.

items.answer: We've gotten very adept at doing this sort of thing. Fundamentally they're all transformer based models, even variants. items.question: How do you think about the latency-throughput tradeoff when optimizing SambaNova's SN40L system for AI inference?
items.object: The latency-throughput tradeoff in AI inference on SambaNova's SN40L system
items.answer: We are optimized for tokens per second because we have this very low latency capability for when you're doing a matrix vector style computation. We do that very quickly, and we're 10x or faster than GPUs at that. Even when you increase the batch size in order to get higher throughput, as you know, there's this latency throughput tradeoff in inference. As you increase the batch size, you get higher throughput, so from the point of view of the server this looks better because it costs you less power per request. You can get higher throughput in terms of the requests that come in. But the latency goes up. If you look at GPUs, the latency really goes up once you get to 24 or above. On an SN40L based system, our latency increases, but it doesn't increase nearly as much. We're still 5x better in terms of latency even at these very high throughputs.

items.object: Tensor parallelism and the latency–throughput tradeoff in inference
items.answer: You still have to deal with the latency, the queuing latency, but the fundamental computation that we can do is more efficient because we can do tensor parallelism in ways that GPUs cannot. GPUs aren't efficient with tensor parallelism because they can't overlap communication very efficiently. We can use tensor parallelism to decrease the time that the overall computation takes, and because we can overlap and hide the latency of communication, this is still effective for us, whereas it might not be, and typically is not, effective if you try and do that on GPUs. items.answer: One of the things that we have because we've got this high capacity memory: we can hold multiple models at the same time, up to 5 trillion parameters in total. items.object: Post-training on SambaNova's architecture
items.answer: Yeah, it supports post-training just fine. In fact, you can post-train very effectively again using this big memory. The benefit of training or even prefill is it's basically compute bound. We've switched from inference, which is memory bound, to training, which is compute bound. Now you're not bandwidth constrained anymore. You can use the big memory to hold lots of parameters. You can do training very effectively because you don't need to hold all of the data in the HBM. You can put part of it in the DDR.

items.question: Which use cases do you see coming to the fore for your architecture?
items.object: Real-time voice and agentic systems as use cases for the architecture
items.answer: What we're seeing is a lot of use cases that are very latency sensitive. Real time voice is one that seems to be something that we've been working with 11Labs and a couple of other companies on, and they really care about low latency. That's one use case that we see, something that we're leaning into. The other use case is these agentic systems that require large numbers of models to coexist at the same time. Using this model switching capability, we can support that with far fewer resources than you would be required if you had to put each of these models on a separate GPU based system. These are the two use cases that seem to be coming to the fore.

items.question: Why do you see dynamic reconfigurable dataflow architectures as an important direction for your research on computing systems for AI?
items.object: Dynamic reconfigurable dataflow architectures for increasingly dynamic AI models
items.answer:
The great thing about being in computer systems, being a computer architect, is that you get influenced by both sides: by where the applications and use cases are going, but also by the constraints of the hardware. In thinking about where the models are going, the models are fundamentally becoming more dynamic. You're getting these mixture of experts style models. You're getting environments where you've got multiple users with different context lengths that need to be served. You're getting models like graph-based neural nets that have a kind of dynamic data access patterns. People are even starting to talk about fine grain sparse tensor computations.

If you think about our current architecture as I described it, taking a graph and mapping it to the machine is a static process. If you think about changing that, it might take you a microsecond or more, maybe a couple microseconds. How about if you fundamentally think about something that's much more dynamic, that can change with much lower latency, or can change just a portion of it? You could potentially dynamically change a portion of the system to execute a different kind of graph. Or maybe you were going to change the size of your tensor. The tensor computation was 1024 by 1024 for the current set of token generations, and now you want to change it to 512 or maybe increase it to 2048. How can you dynamically enable these sorts of things? We're working on an architecture that we call a representation for a dynamic reconfigurable data flow architecture.

If you follow the history of CPU architectures, we started with statically scheduled architectures that we called VLIW, very long instruction word, which were fixed. Eventually they found out those weren't flexible enough, and what you needed was a dynamically scheduled machine, which is what we have today, where the scheduling is all done at runtime. The question is, can we make things more dynamic, more flexible, maybe easier to change? You still want to execute the static case very efficiently, but you want to allow dynamic cases to be implemented with low overhead. That's where we're going from an architecture point of view: can you take these fundamental benefits of reconfigurable data flow architectures and put the D in front of it? Can you make them dynamic with low overhead? You can make anything dynamic, but if you throw away all the advantages, then you haven't solved the problem.

items.question: How do you think about the relationship between software and hardware development in your research on Step Streaming Tensor Programs?
items.object: Software and hardware development in the research on Step Streaming Tensor Programs
items.answer: This is always a sequence of research that involves both how to think about the software and compiler portions of the system, and then how to think about what you should do in terms of the hardware implementation. I've got a couple of really bright PhD students thinking about the hardware. I've got a couple who were working on the software piece. The early software piece has come to fruition, but we haven't said anything about how to do the hardware yet because we don't know precisely how that's going to work.

items.question: How do you think caching should work in agentic AI systems?
items.object: Plan caching in agentic AI systems
items.answer: From a systems point of view, I think about agentic systems as having two components. You're given some high level task that you want to perform, and you give that task to a fairly capable reasoning based LLM like DeepSeek R1, 671 billion parameters, and it comes up with a plan. Then that plan gets executed by a bunch of agents and may access the web. It may invoke a bunch of different specialized LLMs. One of the things we want to do is: how well could we use caching to cache that plan so that it could be reused by subsequent users? That turned out to be a pretty good idea, and we got significant improvements. Caching is an idea that gets used all over the place. But you can't just cache the result. You've got to cache something that's got more semantic content to it than that.

items.question: How do you think about using AI to tackle the compiler challenge for specialized accelerators?
items.object: AI-assisted compiler development for specialized accelerators
items.answer: There's a fundamental problem: accelerators are proliferating for both ML and other kinds of problems because, as you know, everything is energy constrained. The only way to get around this is to become more specialized. Now that you've got this more specialized architecture, you need some sort of programming environment, some sort of compiler to map to it. This is typically the long pole in any systems design. Even from SambaNova's point of view, the most difficult part of the whole endeavor has been delivering the compiler infrastructure for our systems. The question then is, could you use AI to make this problem easier? LLMs are very capable, but they're not as capable as you might think. In particular, they can't really do any search of the space. If you want to make them do search, then you need to add some agentic workflow around them.

items.question: How do you approach using LLMs to create an ML library for a brand-new accelerator architecture?
items.object: Using an agentic system to create ML libraries for new accelerator architectures
items.answer: The space that we want them to be searching is the space of compilers. In particular, the problem that we focused on was how could you take a new architecture, as represented by some low-level representation that we call an architecture specific programming language, and create an ML library. Nvidia has CUDA and cuDNN. What if you wanted to create a new library, for example, that could be targeted by PyTorch for your new architecture? The problem is if you do this, the LLM is not going to be very good at it because it doesn't have any training examples, because this is a brand new architecture. That was the idea. You want to create your new ML library, and you've got your new domain specific architecture with specialized functions, and you want to create your new ML library. We created an agentic system for doing this and an adaptive self-improvement loop around that in order to implement the solution, and it turned out to be a lot better, like three and a half to four times better, than just using an LLM out of the box to try and solve this problem.

items.question: What improvement do you think custom hardware can deliver for agentic AI?
items.object: Custom hardware for agentic AI
items.answer: I think the opportunities are for 5 to 10x improvement in both performance and efficiency. There's a lot of improvement that you can get by using this very fast inference technique. You need ultra low latency inference because you've got multiple LLM calls that you need to make. I think there's a further benefit you get from fast model switching so that you can support these multiple models. You combine these capabilities with the fundamental underlying circuit techniques that we have pioneered at SambaNova to increase energy efficiency and the performance per watt. I think the whole capability will give you a factor of 5 to 10 improvement in performance per watt.
